Metal-Organic Frameworks-Derived Indium-Copper Bimetallic Oxide Catalysts for Selective Aqueous Electroreduction of CO2 Weiwei Guo,a,b Xiaofu Sun,*a,b Chunjun Chen,a,b Dexin Yang,a,b Lu Lu,a,b Youdi Yanga,b and Buxing Han*a,b
MOF-derived In-Cu bimetallic oxides are highly efficient electrocatalysts for transformation of CO2 to CO in aqueous electrolyte. By controlling In-Cu ratios, the Faradaic efficiency of

sections.heading: CO could reach 92.1 %. The excellent performance is mainly attributed to stronger CO2 adsorption, higher electrochemical surface area and lower charge transfer resistance.
sections.text:
Ever since the industrial revolution, the excessive burning of carbon-based fossil fuels has given rise to huge amounts of CO2 emission, which brings about global warming and climate change. Utilizing CO2 as a carbon feedstock for fuels and useful chemicals is very attractive due to the advantages of being abundant, nontoxic, and economical.1-3 In this regard, there is an urgent need to develop sustainable method to convert CO2 into various chemicals. Electroreduction of CO2 in aqueous media, powered by a renewable electricity source, is green, modular and easy for controlling the products of reactions, which is a promising approach.4-6 However, because of the high overpotential for overcoming the energy barriers, the reaction could only occur at high reduction potential in the practical processes.7,8 It causes the formation of H2 and the decease of C-based products selectivity during the reaction.
By comparing the figures of merit of the CO2 reduction processes, the generation of CO via 2e/2H+ reduction is a fundamental reaction for CO2 conversion.9,10 It can be viewed as a key starting material for the synthesis of alcohols and organic acids.11-13 Over the past three decades, several cathode materials have been known to catalyze the reduction of CO2 to CO, such as noble metals (Ag, Au and Pd), metal complexes, 2D materials (N-doped carbon materials and transition-metal dichalcogenides) and single-atom catalysts.1423 Development of the improved catalysts with high activity
and stability is still an important goal to realize the practical and scale-up application. Post-transition metal oxides (PTMOs), like In2O3, SnO2 and Bi2O3, are earth-abundant materials with lower market prices.24-28 They have relatively high overpotential for H2 generation and may be good candidates for CO2 reduction.24 Generally, CO2 electroreduction at PTMOs electrode in aqueous media predominantly produces formate/formic acid,25 because they can hardly bind the CO2•− intermediate.24 In the meantime, PTMOs as the electrocatalyst is hindered by their low rates of product formation and relatively fast cathode deactivation.29,30 Thus, increasing the number of exposed active sites and enhancing the CO2•− adsorption ability are effective ways to improve the CO generation efficiency. Introduction of another active metal into PTMOs may achieve this goal.
Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising materials for gas adsorption31, molecular separation, sensing and heterogeneous catalysis.32,33 One of the most significant advantages of MOFs is that the frameworks are designable and various species of metals and organic linkers can be incorporated, which makes MOFs ideal precursors to prepare desired materials.34 However, MOFs themselves are not suitable electrodes due to the low electrical conductivity and poor stability,34 especially for CO2 reduction (Table S1). Up to date, the most handy and efficient way to overcome these weak points is the thermal decomposition of MOFs under a certain atmosphere (e.g. air, argon).35,36 Therefore, porous bimetallic oxides with desired components and structures can be easily designed for electrochemical applications.
Herein, we report the first work to develop a simple MOFderived method to synthesize porous In-Cu bimetallic oxide catalysts with various Cu/In ratios for CO2 electroreduction. It was discovered that the porous In-Cu bimetallic oxides could be used as efficient and stable electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction to CO in aqueous electrolyte. The tunable CO/H2 ratio has been easily achieved by controlling the In-Cu ratios in the MOF precursors. The maximum Faradaic efficiency of CO could reach 92.1 % with a current density of 11.2 mA cm-2. The excellent catalytic performance of the porous In-Cu bimetallic

Fig. 1 Schematic illustration for preparation process of InCuO.
The procedures to synthesize In-Cu bimetallic oxides catalysts were shown in Fig. 1. Briefly, the initial bimetallic
MOFs were prepared by the reaction of terephthalic acid ligands and metal precursors with different Cu/In molar ratios. According to the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images in Fig. S1, they exhibited needlelike morphologies and the cubes appeared with increasing the proportion of Cu precursor. The structures were confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) fit patterns in Fig. S2, which correspond to crystal structures and well with the data in the previous reports.37,38 Then, the MOFs were calcined at 400 oC in the air for 4 h. The typical thermogravimetric analysis curve can be seen in Fig. S3, and more discussion is provided in the Electronic Supplementary Information. After that, they were electrochemically reduced at -1.4 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) for 20 min to get the final catalysts. The actual In and Cu contents have been shown in Table S2, which were determined by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES). For clarity, InCuO-x is used to stand for the bimetallic oxides catalysts, where x is the Cu/In molar ratio.
Fig. 2 A, B) SEM images of InCuO-0.92. C, D) TEM images of InCuO-0.92. E) HR-TEM image of InCuO-0.92. F, G, H) Elemental mappings and line scanning images of InCuO-0.92. I) XRD patterns of different catalyst. XPS spectra of In 3d (J) and Cu 2p (K) orbits of InCuO-0.92. XPS spectra of In 3d (L) and Cu 2p (M) orbits of InCuO-0.92 before 20 min electroreduction.
SEM images and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images in Fig. 2A-2D show that stacked InCuO-0.92 was formed uniformly and appeared to be a tube-like morphology. High resolution (HR) TEM image in Fig. 2E clearly showed that InCuO-0.92 was composed of In2O3, CuO and Cu2O. The In2O3 specific lattice spacing of (222) facet and (622) facet was 0.290 nm and 0.152 nm, respectively.39 The CuO specific lattice spacing of (111) facet was 0.230 nm.40 The Cu2O specific lattice spacing of (200) facet was 0.209nm.41 All of them agree with the reported values. InCuO-0.92 using elemental distribution mappings (EDS, Fig. 2F), which showed that In (red), Cu (blue) and O (green) were uniformly distributed. Combined with the line scanning images in Fig. 2G-2H, we can conclude InCuO-0.92 is a mixed metal oxide. It was found that the morphology of the In-Cu bimetallic oxides is dependent on the Cu/In ratio in the MOF precursors. As shown in Fig. S4-S8, when the Cu/In atomic ratio is below 0.92, the bimetallic oxides, including In2O3, InCuO-0.15, InCuO0.37, InCuO-0.55, InCuO-0.72, can form a tube-like morphology with a homogeneous distribution of In, Cu and O. Their structures are quite similar and the width of the tube was 200±25 nm. However, the surface of the bimetallic oxides became much rougher and more nubby as the Cu/In ratio continued to increase (Fig. S9). It may be explained that the asprepared In-Cu bimetallic oxide tubes were covered by redundant Cu oxide species.
Moreover, the crystalline structures of In-Cu bimetallic oxides were confirmed by XRD (Fig. 2I). It suggests that Cu oxide and In oxide co-existed in the In-Cu bimetallic oxide catalysts,42,43 which is consistent with the HR-TEM image. The intensity of CuO peaks increased when the proportion of Cu was increased. Besides, very small peaks belong to Cu2O can be found in the XRD patterns,44 indicating Cu2+ species on the oxides surface were partially reduced to Cu+ in the initial electroreduction process.
To get further insight into the chemical composition of this catalyst, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra of InCuO-0.92 were determined (Fig. 2J-2K). The prominent peaks around 444.5 eV and 452.0 eV were assigned to In3+ 3d5/2 and In3+ 3d3/2, respectively,45 which was similar to that of the oxide before initial electroreduction (Fig. 2L). For InCuO-0.92, both Cu2+ and Cu+ can be found. The Cu2+ 2P3/2, Cu2+ 2P1/2, Cu+ 2P3/2 and Cu+ 2P1/2 peaks were centred at 931.9 eV, 951.7 eV, 933.8 eV and 953.9 eV,46 respectively. The spectra also indicate that there was no Cu+ peaks for the oxides before reduction (Fig. 2M). It proved that fractional Cu2+ was reduced to Cu+, which can be also confirmed from the Cu LMM in Auger electron spectroscopy (Fig. S10).47
Besides, the specific surface area of as-prepared In-Cu bimetallic oxides catalysts were determined by BrunauerEmmett-Teller (BET) method (Table S3). It can be seen that the specific surface area increased when the proportion of Cu was increased. InCuO-0.92 has a largest specific surface area (218.4 m2 g-1) with an average pore size of 3.9 nm.
Fig. 3 Electrolysis results in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution (pH = 7.2). A) Faradaic efficiency of CO for different catalysts at the applied potentials. B) Total current density for different catalysts at the applied potentials. C) The long-term stability of InCuO-0.92 at −0.8 V vs. RHE during 24 h electrolysis. D) Tafel plot for CO production over different catalysts. These data were obtained at ambient temperature and pressure with CO2 stream of 2 sccm.
The CO2 electroreduction activities of In-Cu bimetallic oxides were tested using a typical H-type cell with three-electrode system48 in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution (pH 7.2). Controlled potential electrolysis of CO2 was first performed for 2 h at the potential range of -0.5 V to -1.0 V vs. RHE. Gas chromatography (GC) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy were used to quantify the gas and liquid products, respectively. CO and H2 were detected in the gas phase, but no liquid product can be detected in the applied potential range. We also carried out the blank electrolysis experiment over InCuO-0.92 in N2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. Only H2 can be detected, indicating that CO2 was the only carbon source for CO production. As revealed by the Faradaic efficiency for CO production in Fig. 3A, InCuO-0.92 showed higher Faradaic efficiency compared with other catalysts in the whole applied potentials. In particular, InCuO-0.92 reached a maximum Faradaic efficiency of 92.1 %

at the potential of -0.8 V vs. RHE, which is roughly 1.1, 1.3, 1.7, 3.0 and 7.4 times higher than that of InCuO-0.72, InCuO-0.55, InCuO-0.37, InCuO-0.15 and In2O3. In addition, we also summarized the Faradaic efficiency of H2 for the different catalysts in Fig. S11, which has a reverse trend to that of CO. We can conclude that the addition of Cu into the catalyst has a significant impact on the CO2 reduction performance. The increase of Cu content up to a Cu/In atomic ratio of 0.92 can enhance the CO2 reduction activity obviously, indicating the synergistic effect between In oxides and Cu oxides for producing CO. However, when the Cu/In ratio in the catalyst increased further, the Faradaic efficiency for CO production decreased gradually (Fig. S12), and the Faradaic efficiency and the total current density over Cu oxide at the applied potentials was also very low (Fig. S13). It can be ascribed to the fact that more aggregated Cu oxides help to the competitive H2 evolution reaction.49 The total current density for CO2 reduction of over these catalysts is shown in Fig. 3B. It can be seen that the current density of InCuO-0.92 was highest among the catalysts. It can reach 11.2 mA cm-2 at -0.8 V vs. RHE, which is roughly 1.3, 1.7, 2.4, 4.4 and 5.8 times higher than that of InCuO-0.72, InCuO-0.55, InCuO-0.37, InCuO-0.15 and In2O3. The current density in this work is much higher than those In-Cu bimetallic catalysts reported with high Faradaic efficiency (> 90%) (Table S4). Besides, the efficiency for In-Cu bimetallic oxides is also comparable to that of many other MOF-derived materials (Table S5).
The electrochemical stability of the catalysts for CO2 reduction was tested at -0.8 V vs. RHE with an electrolysis time of 2 h, and the total current density did not change obviously with time (Fig. S14). We also investigated a long-term electrode stability of InCuO-0.92 with a 24 h operation (Fig. 3C). There was no obvious decay in current density and Faradaic efficiency of CO, indicating no cathode deactivation
occurred during the period. The long-term stability of InCuO0.92 electrode was also confirmed by SEM, TEM, XPS and Auger spectra (Fig. S15). Furthermore, no obvious change can be observed in the composition, morphology and structure, which further indicates the excellent electrochemical stability of InCuO-0.92.
The semi-situ XPS and semi-situ Auger spectra of InCuO-0.92 were also determined to confirm the change of the valence state during the electrolysis process (Fig. S16). The prominent peaks were assigned to In3+ 3d5/2 and In3+ 3d3/2, respectively (Fig. S16A), which was similar to that of the oxide before used for CO2 electroreduction (Fig. 2L) and after electrolysis (Fig. S15). The spectra of Cu indicate that there was no Cu2+ peaks for the oxides in electrolysis. Cu2+ was reduced to Cu+ and kept stable in reaction. It indicates Cu+ species play an important role in electrolysis. After electrolysis, the valence state of the catalyst was restored.
The variation in partial current density of CO for In-Cu bimetallic oxides was measured as a function of overpotential. The stepped potential electrolysis was performed in CO2saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. The Tafel plot constructed by using these data to gain kinetic insights for CO2 reduction to CO over these electrocatalysts (Fig. 3D). The resulting Tafel slope of InCuO-0.92 was 116.2 mV dec-1, which is smaller than that of InCuO-0.72 (123.8 mV dec-1), InCuO0.55 (131.4 mV dec-1), InCuO-0.37 (136.3 mV dec-1), InCuO0.15 (140.3 mV dec-1) and In2O3 (146.6 mV dec-1), respectively. In addition, the slope of InCuO-0.92 is close to 118 mV dec-1, which indicates a mechanistic pathway in which the first electron transfer step (CO2 + e- → CO2•−) is the ratedetermining step. The other catalysts in our work need higher overpotentials to achieve an initial 1e- transfer process. This mechanism has been invoked for CO2 electroreduction at many metal-based heterogeneous catalysts.50,51

The excellent catalytic activity of InCuO-0.92 can be partially attributed to the large CO2 adsorption capacity. According to the CO2 adsorption isotherms in Fig. 4A, the CO2 adsorption capacity of InCuO-0.92 could reach 59.4 mg g-1 at 25 oC and 1 atm. This value is roughly 1.3, 1.5, 1.7, 2.9 and 5.7 times higher than that of InCuO-0.72, InCuO-0.55, InCuO-0.37, InCuO-0.15 and In2O3, respectively. Large CO2 adsorption capacity is favourable to CO2 conversion.
Based on the Randles-Sevcik equation, the electrochemical activities of In-Cu bimetallic oxides were characterized to gain further insights into the excellent electrocatalytic performance. According to the measured double-layer capacitance in Fig. 4B, the electrochemical active surface area of InCuO-0.92 was estimated to be roughly 1.1, 1.3, 1.8, 4.4 and 6.5 times higher than that of InCuO-0.72, InCuO-0.55, InCuO-0.37, InCuO-0.15 and In2O3, respectively. Larger electrochemical active surface area indicates more active sites, which can be viewed as one of the contributors for the notable enhancement of CO production ability of InCuO-0.92.52,53 The partial current density for CO production was further normalized by electrochemical active surface area (Fig. S17). Similar to the geometric current density, the normalized partial current density of InCuO-0.92 was the highest among the In-Cu bimetallic oxides and the trend is similar to Cu/In ratios. Hence, the different activity for CO2 reduction to CO was mainly attributed to the different In-Cu ratios. We have known only Cu+ species exist in the catalysts. Combined with In oxides, they could first improve the binding strength of CO2 molecules on the surface.24,54 Secondly, InCuO-x with an appropriate Cu content has a stronger adsorption of intermediates (e.g. CO2•−) than In2O3, and Cu+ can dilute negative charge.55 This explains the experimental observation that the Faradaic efficiency for CO production was improved. Therefore, based on the data above, both strong adsorption CO2 reduction intermediates and the high specific surface area can help the production of CO increase.
Furthermore, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured to investigate the properties of electrode/electrolyte interface. We obtained the Nyquist plots by running the experiment at an open circuit potential (Fig. 4C). Then, an equivalent circuit R(C(R(Q(RW)))) was used to fit the high and medium frequency data (Fig. S18). It can be seen that InCuO-0.92 had the lowest interfacial charge transfer resistance (Rct). This ensures a more facile electron transfer in the process of CO2 reduction on InCuO-0.92 electrode surface.56 Our EIS results are in good agreement with the trend of catalytic performance. The results above demonstrate that InCuO-0.92 had advantages in all the crucial steps for CO2 electroreduction to CO.
Based on our results and the related literature, we proposed the possible pathway for the electroreduction of CO2 to CO over In-Cu bimetallic oxides in this work (Fig. S19). First, CO2 is adsorbed and bound on the surface of the electrode. One electron is transferred to CO2 molecule to form CO2•− intermediate, which is the rate-determining step. Then, CO2•− intermediate species continue to be bound and capture the
second electron to form adsorbed CO (COads). Finally, the integral COads is released to form CO.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In summary, the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO was studied over a series of MOF-derived In-Cu bimetallic oxides in 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. It was found that InCuO-0.92 was a very efficient and stable catalyst. The Faradaic efficiency of CO and the total current density could reach as high as 92.1 % and 11.2 mA cm-2, respectively. The detailed study indicated that the superior performance of the catalyst results mainly from the efficient CO2 adsorption, the porous structure for mass diffusion, higher electrochemical surface area, stronger CO2 adsorption, lower charge transfer resistance, as well as the synergistic effect between In oxides and Cu oxides. We believe that some other efficient catalysts can be designed using PTMOs for CO2 electroreduction.
